subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: A→B and g: B→A are two functions such that gof = I_A and fog = I_B, then prove that (i) f is a bijection and (ii) g = f⁻¹.

mark_split.label: Prove f is one one and onto
Show g and f⁻¹ share a domain
Show they agree at every point

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.98 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 142. SECTION: the heading reads "FUNCTIONS LAQ", so the SECTION here is the book's, not ours — this is the one place in the bank that names a section. The book supplies the section only, never a mark split. Printed appearances: TS 15 · AP 18. A pure theory proof, and the converse of Unit 1's answer 4 — there f was GIVEN bijective; here bijectivity is what has to be established. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Quote the two composition results
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks. Two standard results do all the work: if gof is one one then the FIRST function is one one, and if gof is onto then the SECOND is onto. Write both before using either.
steps.memory_tip: Two standard results: gof one one makes the FIRST function one one; gof onto makes the SECOND onto.
lines: (i) To show f is a bijection, we use:
(a) If gof is one one, then f is one one.
(b) If gof is onto, then g is onto.
I_A and I_B are identity functions, so both are

steps.why: The two results point in opposite directions — one gives information about f, the other about g. Both hypotheses are needed to pin f down completely.
common_mistakes: Assuming f is a bijection rather than proving it.
Applying result (a) to g instead of f.

steps.label: Prove f is one one and onto
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. gof = I_A is one one, so by (a) f is one one. fog = I_B is onto, so by (b) f is onto — note it is fog, not gof, that gives this half.
steps.memory_tip: gof = I_A gives f one one, but it is fog = I_B that gives f onto. Different composition each half.
lines: gof = I_A is one one ⇒ f is one one   [by (a)]
fog = I_B is onto ⇒ f is onto   [by (b), with the
roles of f and g exchanged in fog]
∴ f is both one one and onto, hence a bijection.

recall.must_convey: That gof being one one gives f one one, and fog being onto gives f onto — so f is a bijection.

steps.why: In fog the FIRST function is g and the second is f — so result (b), which is about the second function, gives f onto. Reading which composition is which is the only thing to watch here.
common_mistakes: Concluding g is a bijection instead of f.

steps.label: Show g and f⁻¹ share a domain
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Two functions are equal only if they have the same domain AND agree everywhere. This step settles the domain half.
steps.memory_tip: Equality of functions needs the domain too: g and f⁻¹ both run B→A.
lines: Given g: B→A.  Since f: A→B is a bijection,
∴ g and f⁻¹ both have domain B.

recall.must_convey: That g and f⁻¹ are both functions from B to A, so they share a domain.

steps.why: f⁻¹ only exists because part (i) proved f bijective. The two parts of this question are not independent — the second needs the first.
common_mistakes: Claiming f⁻¹ exists without reference to part (i).

steps.label: Show they agree at every point
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. Take any b in B, let g(b) = a, and use fog = I_B to show f(a) = b — which is exactly what f⁻¹(b) = a means.
steps.memory_tip: Take ANY b, set g(b) = a, and use fog = I_B to get f(a) = b — which is exactly f⁻¹(b) = a.
lines: Let b ∈ B and g(b) = a, where a ∈ A.
So g(b) = a = f⁻¹(b) for every b ∈ B.

recall.must_convey: That for any b, g(b) = a gives f(a) = b via fog = I_B, so f⁻¹(b) = a = g(b), hence g = f⁻¹.

steps.why: Two functions are equal when they agree at EVERY point, so the argument has to start with an arbitrary b — not a particular one.
common_mistakes: Using gof where fog is needed.

insider_note: Both quoted results are needed and they point at different functions: gof being one-one gives f one-one, but the onto half must come from fog, not from gof. Part (ii) is then a separate domain-and-value proof.
